summary: Fort Bragg sits on a dramatic stretch of Mendocino Coast headlands where you can stand on coastal bluffs and watch gray whales migrate without binoculars — and where the famous Glass Beach, its shore smoothed from decades of sea-glass tumbling, draws visitors from around the world to a place that barely spans 2.9 square miles. That tiny footprint holds a remarkably self-contained town: the Georgia-Pacific lumber mill site that once anchored the economy is being remediated into a massive coastal trail and open-space project, while Mendocino Coast District Hospital, the local school system, and a modest tourism-driven hospitality sector now form the employment backbone. The affordability math is stark — a median home price of $481,200 against a median household income of $53,580 yields a price-to-income ratio near 9:1, well above what conventional lending considers comfortable, while rents averaging $1,264 consume roughly 28% of that same median income. The climate is startlingly even: annual daytime highs average just 62°F with lows around 48°F, meaning fog-cooled summers that rarely crack 70 and mild winters without frost — sunscreen-optional weather year-round. Highway 1 is effectively the only corridor in or out, threading south to Mendocino village and north toward Eureka, making this emphatically not a commuter suburb of anywhere. The compact downtown along Franklin Street holds independent restaurants, a brewery, coffee shops, and a genuine working-fishing-harbor atmosphere that no coastal resort town could replicate. Fort Bragg is a place where the ocean is omnipresent and the isolation is the point — but that same remoteness means limited employers, limited healthcare options, and a housing market increasingly pressured by outside demand against modest local wages.
